criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and falls under Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper studies river-basin Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) institutions (Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council) managing surface-water resources and commercial/irrigation allocations; the author explicitly notes that rural primary water supply and sanitation remained the separate domain of Rural District Councils and that the studied catchment councils focused almost exclusively on surface water and commercial water use. The Pungwe-Mutare interbasin transfer scheme and brief mentions of primary water gaps serve only as contextual background to catchment-level governance politics.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 because it examines legal, institutional, and governance arrangements under Zimbabwe's 1998 Water Act (devolution to Catchment and Sub-Catchment Councils, stakeholder representation, inter-agency coordination with local authorities and ZINWA, and raw-water abstraction permits/levies); however, plain_criterion2_decision is still 'exclude' because the study fails Criteria 1 and 4 as a river-basin water-resource management study rather than a water or sanitation service-access study. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper FAILS Criterion 2 (c2_legal_admin_factor = 'no') because the governance factors analysed concern macro/meso catchment-council formation, stakeholder representation, inter-agency catchment planning, and commercial/irrigation raw-water permits rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (even Box 1's 1500 L/day primary threshold and permit levy rule concerns micro-scale agricultural irrigation in the Gatsi irrigation scheme and is analysed in relation to gaining seats on the Sub-Catchment Council).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3 as a qualitative empirical case study drawing on primary observation of Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council meetings, interviews with councillors and local/sector officials, and review of council attendance records, although no standalone methodology section is provided.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Reported outcomes are catchment-level institutional governance processes—preliminary catchment outline planning coordination, councillor gender/sector representation (e.g., 0% women on Save CC and 20% on Pungwe SCC), meeting attendance (Mutare City Council missing over 90% of Save CC meetings), and compliance/conflict resolution among commercial and irrigation raw-water permit holders—rather than household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, continuity, affordability, or disconnection outcomes.
criterion_notes.c5: Institutional unit of analysis (Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council) and qualitative case-study design are identifiable, but the paper lacks a methods section reporting sampling, interview counts, or observation protocols, and no household/community service-access population, rule-type service-access exposure, or service-access outcome is measured.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study (primary observation of council meetings, interviews with councillors and officials, and review of council records)
country: Zimbabwe (Save Catchment Area / Pungwe River Basin, with transboundary context involving Mozambique)
population_and_sample: Catchment-level water-resource governance institutions in eastern Zimbabwe (Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council, plus local authority and sector officials; exact sample sizes of interviewees and observed meetings not reported)
exposure: Implementation of Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM) and integrated catchment management under Zimbabwe's 1998 Water Act (devolution to Catchment and Sub-Catchment Councils, stakeholder representation, raw-water allocation permits and commercial water levies, and fast-track land resettlement pressures)
outcome: Catchment-level institutional governance processes: inter-agency coordination in catchment outline planning, stakeholder and gender representation on councils, meeting attendance, and compliance/conflict resolution over commercial and irrigation raw-water allocations
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic — river-basin Integrated Water Resources Management / water-resource governance study unrelated to household or community water or sanitation service access, per Exclusion Criterion 7; also fails narrow Criterion 2 and Criterion 4). Using interviews, meeting observations, and council records in Zimbabwe's Save Catchment Area, Tapela (2002) examines institutional challenges facing the Save Catchment Council and Pungwe Sub-Catchment Council—inter-agency coordination, stakeholder and gender representation on councils, commercial farmer dominance, and conflict resolution over commercial/irrigation raw-water permits. Primary domestic water supply and sanitation (managed separately by Rural District Councils) are not empirically evaluated, and no household or community service-access outcomes are reported; thus the study is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
